blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
Introduction
This publication on WHO recommendations related to maternal health is one of four in a series; 
the others relate to newborn, child and adolescent health. The objective of this document is to 
make available WHO recommendations on maternal health in one easy-to-access document 
for WHO staff, policy-makers, programme managers, and health professionals. The compilation 
can also help better define gaps to prioritize guideline updates. 
This document is meant to respond to the questions:
■What health interventions should be delivered during pregnancy, childbirth and the
postnatal pe

summary.text: Introduces a compilation of WHO maternal health recommendations, one of a four-part series, aimed at WHO personnel, policy-makers, programme managers and health practitioners and to help identify gaps for updating guidelines. Explains how WHO develops guidelines using GRADE ratings of evidence quality and a structured evidence-to-decision framework leading to strong or conditional recommendations, and notes that items are flagged as New or Update relative to 2013.

blocks.title: Nutritional supplements
blocks.content:
■
■Counselling about healthy eating and keeping physically active during pregnancy is 
recommended for pregnant women to stay healthy and to prevent excessive weight gain 
during pregnancy. (Recommended). Source 
■
■In undernourished populations, nutrition education on increasing daily energy and protein 
intake is recommended for pregnant women to reduce the risk of low-birth-weight neonates.
(Context-specific recommendation). Source 
■
■In undernourished populations, balanced energy and protein dietary supplementation is 
recommended for pregnant women to reduce the risk of stillbirths and s

summary.text: Lists WHO antenatal recommendations on diet and supplements, including counselling on healthy eating and activity, energy and protein measures in undernourished populations, daily or weekly iron and folic acid, and calcium where intake is low. Vitamin A and zinc are advised only in specific contexts, multiple micronutrients and vitamins B6, C, D and E are not recommended, and lowering caffeine intake is advised for heavy consumers.

blocks.title: Maternal and fetal assessment
blocks.content:
Anaemia	
■
■Full blood count testing is the recommended method for diagnosing anaemia in pregnancy. 
In settings where full blood count testing is not available, on-site haemoglobin testing with 
a haemoglobinometer is recommended over the use of the haemoglobin colour scale as the 
method for diagnosing anaemia in pregnancy. (Context-specific recommendation). Source 
Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)	
■
■Midstream urine culture is the recommended method for diagnosing asymptomatic 
bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnancy. In settings where urine culture is not available, on-site 
midstream urine Gram-sta

summary.text: Sets out recommended antenatal assessments, including preferred tests for anaemia and asymptomatic bacteriuria, classifying hyperglycaemia found in pregnancy, HIV testing and counselling, TB screening in high-prevalence settings, and asking about intimate partner violence, tobacco and other substance use. It also states that routine cardiotocography, Doppler scans and replacing palpation with fundal-height measurement are not recommended, kick-chart counting only in research, and one ultrasound before 24 weeks is advised.

blocks.title: Preventive measures
blocks.content:
Antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)	
■
■A seven-day antibiotic regimen is recommended for all pregnant women with asymptomatic 
bacteriuria (ASB) to prevent persistent bacteriuria, preterm birth and low birth weight. 
(Recommended). Source 
Antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections (RUTI)	
■
■Antibiotic prophylaxis is only recommended to prevent recurrent urinary tract infections 
in pregnant women in the context of rigorous research. (Context-specific recommendation/
research). Source 
Antenatal anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis	
■
■Antenatal prophylaxis

summary.text: Lists preventive measures in pregnancy, such as a seven-day antibiotic course for asymptomatic bacteriuria, deworming in endemic areas after the first trimester, tetanus toxoid and influenza vaccination, bed nets and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine preventive treatment against malaria. Anti-D prophylaxis and antibiotics for recurrent urinary infections are reserved for research, and the section also covers primaquine use to prevent vivax or ovale malaria relapse according to G6PD status and oral PrEP for pregnant women at substantial HIV risk.

blocks.title: Interventions for common physiological symptoms
blocks.content:
Nausea and vomiting	
■
■Ginger, chamomile, vitamin B6 and/or acupuncture are recommended for the relief of nausea 
in early pregnancy, based on a woman’s preferences and available options. (Recommended).
Source 
Heartburn	
■
■Advice on diet and lifestyle is recommended to prevent and relieve heartburn in pregnancy. 
Antacid preparations can be offered to women with troublesome symptoms that are not 
relieved by lifestyle modification. (Recommended). Source 
Leg cramps	
■
■Magnesium, calcium or non-pharmacological treatment options can be used for the 
relief of leg cramps in pregnancy, based o

summary.text: Gives recommended options for common pregnancy discomforts, including ginger, chamomile, vitamin B6 or acupuncture for nausea and diet and lifestyle advice or antacids for heartburn. It also covers leg cramps, low back and pelvic pain, constipation, and varicose veins and oedema, with choices guided by the woman's preferences and what is available.

Group antenatal care

summary.text: Lists health-system recommendations for antenatal care, including women carrying their own case notes, midwife-led continuity of care, group antenatal care in research settings, women's group participatory learning cycles, and community mobilization with home visits. It also covers task shifting of health promotion and supplement distribution to various cadres, measures to recruit and keep health workers in rural areas, and a schedule of at least eight antenatal contacts.

blocks.title: Prevention of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
blocks.content:
PREVENTION OF PRE-ECLAMPSIA AND ECLAMPSIA
■
■In populations with low dietary calcium intake, daily calcium supplementation (1.5–2.0 g 
oral elemental calcium) is recommended for pregnant women to reduce the risk of pre-
eclampsia. (Context-specific recommendation). Source 
■
■Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin, 75 mg) is recommended for the prevention of pre-
eclampsia in women at high risk of developing the condition. (Strong recommendation, 
moderate quality evidence). Source
■
■	Low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin, 75 mg) for the prevention of pre-eclampsia and 
its related complicat

summary.text: Sets out recommendations on preventing pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, including calcium supplements where intake is low, low-dose aspirin for high-risk women started before 20 weeks, and treating severe hypertension. Home rest, strict bed rest, salt restriction and diuretics such as thiazides are not recommended for this purpose.

blocks.title: Interventions to improve preterm birth outcomes
blocks.content:
INTERVENTIONS TO IMPROVE PRETERM BIRTH OUTCOMES
NEW
Antenatal corticosteroids to improve newborn outcomes	
■
■Antenatal corticosteroid therapy is recommended for women at risk of preterm birth from 
24 weeks to 34 weeks of gestation when the following conditions are met:
—
— gestational age assessment can be accurately undertaken;
—
— preterm birth is considered imminent;
—
— there is no clinical evidence of maternal infection;
—
— adequate childbirth care is available (including the capacity to recognize and safely 
manage preterm labour and birth);
—
— the preterm newborn can receive adequat

summary.text: Presents new recommendations to improve outcomes of preterm birth, centred on antenatal corticosteroids for women at risk between 24 and 34 weeks when conditions such as accurate dating, imminent birth, no maternal infection and adequate maternal and newborn care are met. It specifies use in multiple pregnancies, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, hypertensive disorders, fetal growth restriction and diabetes, names dexamethasone or betamethasone as the drugs of choice, allows one repeat course, and excludes chorioamnionitis and planned late-preterm caesarean section. It also advises against tocolytics, routine antibiotics with intact membranes and routine caesarean delivery, while recommending magnesium sulfate before 32 weeks and antibiotics such as erythromycin after membrane rupture, but not co-amoxiclav.

blocks.title: Prevention of maternal peripartum infections
blocks.content:
PREVENTION OF MATERNAL PERIPARTUM INFECTIONS 
NEW
■
■Routine perineal/pubic shaving prior to giving vaginal birth is not recommended. (Conditional 
recommendation based on very low-quality evidence). Source
■
■Digital vaginal examination at intervals of four hours is recommended for routine assessment 
of active first stage of labour in low-risk women. (Strong recommendation based on very low-
quality evidence). Source
■
■Routine vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine during labour for the purpose of preventing 
infectious morbidities is not recommended. (Strong recommendation based on moderate-

summary.text: Lists new recommendations on preventing maternal infections around childbirth, advising against routine shaving, chlorhexidine vaginal cleansing and routine antibiotics in situations such as preterm labour with intact membranes, term membrane rupture, meconium, operative vaginal birth, episiotomy and uncomplicated birth. Antibiotics are recommended for GBS colonization, preterm membrane rupture, manual placenta removal, severe perineal tears and caesarean section, given before incision as a single dose of first-generation cephalosporin or penicillin, with povidone-iodine vaginal cleansing beforehand.

blocks.title: Induction of labour
blocks.content:
When induction of labour may be appropriate
■
■Induction of labour is recommended for women who are known with certainty to have 
reached 41 weeks (>40 weeks + 7 days) of gestation. (Weak recommendation, low quality of 
evidence). Source
■
■Induction of labour is not recommended in women with an uncomplicated pregnancy at 
gestational age less than 41 weeks. (Weak recommendation, low quality of evidence). Source
■
■If gestational diabetes is the only abnormality, induction of labour before 41 weeks of 
gestation is not recommended. (Weak recommendation, very low quality evidence). Source
■
■In

summary.text: Sets out recommendations on when to induce labour, such as at 41 completed weeks or after prelabour membrane rupture at term, but not for uncomplicated pregnancies before 41 weeks, gestational diabetes alone or suspected macrosomia. Recommended methods include oral or low-dose vaginal misoprostol (not after previous caesarean), vaginal prostaglandins, balloon catheter with or without oxytocin and membrane sweeping, with betamimetics for uterine hyperstimulation and outpatient induction not recommended.

blocks.title: Delay in the first stage of labour
blocks.content:
NEW
■
■Active phase partograph with a four-hour action line is recommended for monitoring the 
progress of labour. (Quality of evidence low, Strength of recommendation strong). Source
■
■Digital vaginal examination at intervals of four hours is recommended for routine assessment 
and identification of delay in active labour. (Quality of evidence very low, Strength of 
recommendation weak). Source
Prevention of delay in the first stage of labour	
NEW
■
■A package of care for active management of labour for prevention of delay in labour is not 
recommended. (Quality of evidence low, Strength of

summary.text: Presents new recommendations on monitoring and managing delay in the first stage of labour, including a partograph with a four-hour action line and four-hourly vaginal examinations, with active management packages, early amniotomy, routine oxytocin, antispasmodics, intravenous fluids and enemas not recommended for prevention. Oral intake, mobility, upright positions and continuous companionship are encouraged, and for confirmed delay oxytocin alone or with amniotomy is recommended, but not oral misoprostol, high-dose regimens or internal tocodynamometry.

blocks.title: Prevention of postpartum haemorrhage
blocks.content:
PREVENTION OF POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE (PPH)
■
■The use of uterotonics for the prevention of PPH during the third stage of labour is 
recommended for all births. (Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Source
■
■Oxytocin (10 IU, IV/IM) is the recommended uterotonic drug for the prevention of PPH. 
(Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Source
■
■In settings where oxytocin is unavailable, the use of other injectable uterotonics (if 
appropriate ergometrine/methylergometrine or the fixed drug combination of oxytocin

WHO RECOMMENDATIONS ON MATERNAL HEALTH
and ergometrin

summary.text: Sets out recommendations to prevent postpartum haemorrhage, chiefly a uterotonic for every birth with oxytocin preferred, alternatives such as ergometrine or oral misoprostol where oxytocin is unavailable, and misoprostol given by community and lay health workers where no skilled attendant is present. It also covers controlled cord traction depending on attendant availability, late rather than early cord clamping, no sustained uterine massage after oxytocin, routine uterine tone checks, and oxytocin and cord traction in caesarean section.

blocks.title: Postnatal care
blocks.content:
POSTNATAL CARE
Timing of discharge from the health facility
■
■After an uncomplicated vaginal birth in a health facility, healthy mothers and newborns 
should receive care in the facility for at least 24 hours after birth. (Weak recommendation, 
low quality evidence). Source
Timing and number of postnatal contacts
■
■If birth is in a health facility, mothers and newborns should receive postnatal care in the 
facility for at least 24 hours after birth. Source
■
■If birth is at home, the first postnatal contact should be as early as possible within 24 hours 
of birth. Source
■
■At least three ad

summary.text: Sets out WHO recommendations on postnatal care, including a stay of at least 24 hours in the facility after an uncomplicated birth and a schedule of at least four postnatal contacts, with home visits in the first week. It describes how the mother should be assessed in the first day and at later contacts, covering bleeding, vital signs, recovery, breastfeeding, mood, depression and signs of domestic abuse. It also lists counselling topics, warning signs to report, nutrition advice with iron and folic acid supplementation, and psychosocial support, family planning, hygiene and exercise.

blocks.title: . Health promotion for maternal and newborn health
blocks.content:
HEALTH PROMOTION FOR MATERNAL AND NEWBORN HEALTH 
NEW
Birth Preparedness and Complication Readiness	
■
■Birth Preparedness and Complication Readiness interventions are recommended to increase 
the use of skilled care at birth and to increase the timely use of facility care for obstetric and 
newborn complications. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence). Additional 
research is required. Source
Male involvement interventions for MNH	
■
■Interventions to promote the involvement of men during pregnancy, childbirth and 
after birth are recommended to facilitate and support improved

summary.text: Lists WHO recommendations on health promotion for maternal and newborn health, such as birth preparedness, involving men, maternity waiting homes, community transport schemes, partnership with traditional birth attendants and a companion of choice during labour. It also recommends community engagement through women's groups and community participation in quality improvement and programme planning, and calls for more research on community roles in maternal death surveillance and on rights awareness.

blocks.title: Postpartum haemorrhage
blocks.content:
TREATMENT OF POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE3
■
■Intravenous oxytocin alone is the recommended uterotonic drug for the treatment of PPH.
(Strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Source
■
■If intravenous oxytocin is unavailable, or if the bleeding does not respond to oxytocin, the 
use of intravenous ergometrine, oxytocin-ergometrine fixed dose, or a prostaglandin drug 
(including sublingual misoprostol, 800 µg) is recommended. (Strong recommendation, low 
quality evidence). Source
■
■The use of isotonic crystalloids is recommended in preference to the use of colloids for the 
initial intrave

summary.text: Sets out WHO recommendations for treating postpartum haemorrhage, starting with intravenous oxytocin and alternative uterotonics, crystalloid fluids, tranexamic acid and uterine massage. It then covers escalating and temporizing measures such as balloon tamponade, embolization, surgery, bimanual or aortic compression and anti-shock garments, along with the management of retained placenta. The block ends with the first recommendations on pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, favouring magnesium sulfate over other anticonvulsants.

summary.text: Continues WHO recommendations on severe pre-eclampsia, covering when to induce labour, when expectant management is acceptable by gestational age, and early delivery at term. It also recommends continuing or starting antihypertensive treatment after birth and advises against corticosteroids specifically for HELLP syndrome.

■A simple regimen such as ampicillin and once-daily gentamicin is recommended as first-

summary.text: Recommends first-line antibiotic regimens for chorioamnionitis (ampicillin with once-daily gentamicin) and for postpartum endometritis (clindamycin with gentamicin).

blocks.title: HIV infection
blocks.content:
HIV diagnosis
■
■Couples and partners in antenatal care settings should be offered voluntary HIV testing 
and counselling with support for mutual disclosure. (Strong recommendation, low quality 
evidence). Source
Generalized epidemics
■
■Provider-initiated testing and counselling is recommended for women as a routine 
component of the package of care in all antenatal, childbirth, postpartum and paediatric 
care settings. (No strength, no quality of evidence). Source quoted also in Source
■
■Re-testing is recommended in the third trimester, or during labour or shortly after delivery, 
because o

summary.text: Sets out WHO recommendations on HIV in pregnant and breastfeeding women, starting with couple testing and provider-initiated testing in generalized and low-level epidemics. It covers when to start antiretroviral therapy, practices to reduce transmission during labour and delivery, non-stigmatizing care, and follow-up of mothers and HIV-exposed infants. It also names the preferred first-line ART regimen, infant prophylaxis by feeding type, and advises against vitamin A supplementation to reduce mother-to-child transmission.

blocks.title: Malaria
blocks.content:
NEW
Treating uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in special risk groups
First trimester of pregnancy
■
■Treat pregnant women with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria during the first trimester 
with 7 days of quinine + clindamycin. (Strong recommendation). Source
Pregnant and breastfeeding women
■
■In women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, consider weekly chemoprophylaxis with 
chloroquine until delivery and breastfeeding are completed, then, on the basis of G6PD 
status, treat with primaquine to prevent future relapse. (Conditional recommendation, 
moderate-quality evidence). Source

summary.text: Gives WHO recommendations for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in the first trimester (seven days of quinine plus clindamycin) and for chloroquine chemoprophylaxis in pregnant or breastfeeding women, followed by primaquine depending on G6PD status.

blocks.title: Tuberculosis
blocks.content:
NEW
Nutritional Care and support for patients with tuberculosis
■
■Pregnant women with active TB and moderate undernutrition, or with inadequate weight 
gain, should be provided with locally available nutrient rich or fortified supplementary foods, 
as necessary to achieve an average weekly minimum weight gain of approximately 300 g in 
the second and third trimesters. (Strong recommendation, very low quality of evidence)
■
■Patients with active multidrug-resistant TB and moderate undernutrition should be provided 
with locally available nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods, as neces

summary.text: Sets out WHO recommendations on nutritional care for pregnant and lactating women with active tuberculosis, including fortified or supplementary foods to reach a target weekly weight gain. It also recommends multiple micronutrient supplements with iron and folic acid, and calcium to prevent pre-eclampsia where intake is low.
